title: KrMM Recurrences: HPC-Enhanced Estimators for Nonlinear Classical Shadows
authors: Matthias Gruber, Sabrina Herbst, Ivona Brandic, Vincenzo De Maio
abstract: While quantum technologies are rapidly evolving, near-term applications heavily rely on hybrid quantum-classical paradigms. Among these, the classical shadows framework has gained a lot of traction, not only for quantum information science, but also for the development and verification of quantum hardware. It allows to efficiently classically estimate many properties of quantum states from randomized measurements alone, a task that is otherwise intractable due to the destructive nature of measurements in quantum systems. There are, however, many properties of interest that are, due to their very problem formulation, not efficiently estimable. In this work, we identify a computational kernel occurring in estimators of polynomial functions, a class of problems that are in general computationally difficult to solve. We show that this structure allows a row-wise partition that, together with a custom SIMD vectorization, enables massive parallelization and can reduce the computational cost significantly. We show applicability and scalability of the approach on different tasks, and our results showcase that the approach allows high sequential throughput and close-to-ideal parallel scaling. The work thus provides a new way of identifying and exploiting structure in classical shadow estimators, resulting in practical advantages on inherently difficult problems.
summary: This paper introduces a novel, highly parallel computational technique to estimate difficult nonlinear properties of quantum states using classical shadows. By mapping the estimation problem onto a structured Kronecker-matrix-matrix recurrence, the authors enable massive parallelization via row-wise decomposition and custom SIMD optimization. This significantly boosts the throughput for tasks like QFI estimation, making previously computationally prohibitive quantum characterization feasible on modern HPC hardware.
main_problem: The paper addresses the computational bottleneck in estimating nonlinear properties of quantum states using the classical shadows formalism, which is otherwise intractable.
main_result: By identifying a recurring computational kernel structured as Kronecker-matrix-matrix (KrMM) recurrences, the authors enable massive parallelization via row-wise partitioning and custom SIMD vectorization.
method: The core method involves reformulating polynomial estimators into KrMM recurrences, which are then decomposed into independent row-wise Kronecker-matrix-vector (KrMV) recurrences for parallel processing.
model_or_system: The work analyzes quantum states ($ho$) and their properties, utilizing the classical shadows framework derived from randomized measurements on quantum systems.
key_observables: Nonlinear properties such as purity and Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) are key observables being estimated.
important_parameters: The complexity scales are analyzed concerning the number of measurements ($N$), the order of the polynomial ($k$), and the number of qubits ($n$).
main_assumptions: The approach assumes that the estimators can be mapped onto a structured recurrence relation (KrMM) that allows for row-wise decomposition.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison between plain and batch classical shadows, and detail the implementation of the fused row kernel using custom SIMD data layouts for high parallel efficiency.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the classical shadows framework and the difficulty of nonlinear estimation. It then derives the KrMM recurrence structure, details the row-wise decomposition and custom hardware implementation (SIMD/SRM), and finally benchmarks the approach on specific tasks like QFI estimation, showing scaling results.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, high-performance computational tool for characterizing quantum states that goes beyond simple expectation values, directly impacting the feasibility of verifying quantum hardware properties.

Fig. 2: Overview of Plain and Batch Classical Shadows. On the left (orange), quantum measurements are collected by randomly sampling a unitary U from the ensemble U. The process is repeated N times, and the measurements {(Ui, |b⟩i)} are forwarded to the classical computer for post-processing. For the plain shadows (top), the estimator for the k-th order polynomial is then built by iterating over all size-k subsets of the snapshots, scaling as O(N k). For batch shadows (bottom), the snapshots are split into NB ≥k distinct batches.
